accounting: Organize programs for downstream hierarchical work-remaining accounting. A program is a durable work-policy package, not merely a topic, method, result, or submission. Create the smallest accounting tree sufficient for future contribution attribution. Split work when credible future contributions could independently activate, stop, solve, prune, or materially change the remaining work of one package without the other. Do not split merely because a submission contains multiple claims, methods, computations, or intermediate results. When several separately estimable work packages directly advance the same narrower objective, create or reuse that objective as their parent and place the packages beneath it. The parent retains only genuine integration or coordination work. Place a program beneath the narrowest existing program whose objective it directly advances. Do not infer accounting ancestry solely from mathematical or evidentiary dependency. Preserve existing topology when a later submission strengthens, reproduces, or supplies additional evidence for an existing work package. Do not automatically create unstructured-search nodes, unary grouping programs, or one program per intermediate result. Use these principles only to organize topology; do not estimate probabilities, hours, remaining work, or credit. In topologyRationale, state the shared activation event represented by each new parent, what could make sibling packages activate, stop, or change separately, and why apparently distinct material was consolidated.
workedExample: Worked structural examples follow. These examples teach accounting boundaries, not subject-matter labels. Example A — portfolio and leaves: a project seeks to certify an optimizer. One credible work package derives data-reduction invariants; another develops a convergence certificate. Both activate when the optimizer-certification portfolio is pursued, but either can be completed, pruned, or accelerated without the other. Represent one optimizer-certification portfolio program with two leaf programs beneath it, and attach each accepted intermediate result to the appropriate leaf. The portfolio retains only integration work. Example B — consolidate results: one submission proves a lemma and supplies a computation that both advance the same data-reduction work package. They may be distinct intermediate results, but they do not by themselves create distinct programs. Example C — dependency is not ancestry: a convergence result cites a data-reduction result, but convergence work has its own activation and stopping condition. Keep the work packages as siblings beneath their shared portfolio and express the mathematical dependency between intermediate results. Example D — preserve topology: a later submission strengthens the convergence certificate. Update the existing convergence leaf and its result or add a reusable result there; do not create a program named for the later submission. Internal programs are portfolio containers and leaf programs are thread-equivalent accounting work packages, but both remain entities of kind program. Do not reproduce this example mechanically: choose the smallest accounting-sufficient topology justified by the actual accepted evidence.
